# Decision history — lege-ecosystem

Every revision of every decision, plus the terminal revisions of other normative records. Includes archived records: this is the project's memory of what it used to think.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.a-fold-may-not-change-a-letters-counters

### Revision 1 — Truetyping never folds shapes that enclose different counters, and a stroke is far even when it is a hairline

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.a-fold-may-not-change-a-letters-counters/1` · scope `path "lege-process/encoding/bitrows.rs"`, `path "lege-process/encoding/glyphfont.rs"`

Two gates now guard the glyph dictionary against folding one letter into another. First, topology: a shape's enclosed counters are counted (`holes`, a flood fill from the border) and no match is considered across a different count — `c` never becomes `e`, `h` never becomes `b`, `a` never becomes `u`. The count is only trusted where the strokes have an interior, because a wall one pixel thick is opened or closed by a single speck. Second, the strict gate gained the far-pixel test the tolerant gate already had: ink that has none of the other shape's within a pixel of it, capped at 1% of the ink (minimum 2) with no far group larger than 2. A change of impression puts its difference along the strokes it thickens, so it is never far; a stroke one shape has and the other lacks is far along its length, however thin it is. Strict matches are also ranked by that structural agreement first, so rejecting a candidate never hands the instance to a worse one that survived.

**Context.** A user's own run of the ITU T.88 specification came back with `which` as `wbicb`, `the` as `tbe`, `decoded` as `deeoded`, `are` as `ure` — whole letters replaced, in body text, in the format that had just been made the default. The fold dump showed why: the tolerant gate forgives ink within a pixel of the other shape, and at reading sizes the crossbar of an `e` is four pixels long with both ends touching the bowl, so only two pixels are left to notice. `far_blob <= 3` was meant to catch a missing stroke and cannot, because a stroke at that size is not three pixels of anything. The strict gate had no far test at all: its 2x2-block measure sees nothing in a one-pixel hairline, so it merged `a` with `e` and `u` with `n` on a heavier face.

**Consequences.** Dictionaries grow: 3 pages of Gobineau 150 to 160 shapes, 5 pages of T.88 372 to 414, 5 pages of the Gernet scan 443 to 465 — 3-10%, and the fonts with them. Splitting is the safe direction: two prototypes for one letter cost bytes, one prototype for two letters costs the reader the word. Counters are computed per component (a flood fill alongside the ink profile) and prune candidates, so the tolerant stage got faster rather than slower. A scan whose counter is filled in by heavy ink now keeps its own prototype instead of folding; that is a split, not a substitution. Text on a source that was already binarized at low resolution still merges touching pairs (`in` reads as `m`), which no pixel budget separates at ten pixels a letter.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.annotator-abandon-takes-pp-label

### Revision 1 — Liminal Annotator: a YOLO abandon box takes PP-DocLayout-L's label for the same region

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.annotator-abandon-takes-pp-label/1` · scope `path "lege-misc/liminal-annotator/**"`

When a teacher-pool folder is pre-filled from DocLayout-YOLO, each abandon box takes the label of the best-overlapping PP-DocLayout-L detection (PP score >= 0.15, IoU >= 0.3), keeping YOLO's geometry and recording both labels in provenance. Older projects get the same pass once on the next folder open, as one undoable bulk change; hand-converted boxes are untouched. Only unmatched boxes stay in the abandon holding class.

**Context.** The first import kept every YOLO abandon box as abandon and used PP only as a comparison layer, so 452,569 boxes (about 2 per page) needed manual conversion although PP had a labelled box for most. On a 1-in-8 sample, PP >= 0.30/IoU 0.5 resolves 92.8%, PP >= 0.15/IoU 0.3 resolves 97.5% with the same label mix; a containment fallback adds 0.9% but risks labelling page numbers as text, so it was not used.

**Consequences.** On the user's pool project the pass labelled 441,661 of 452,569 abandon boxes in 17 s; 10,908 remain on 9,581 pages. PP's own errors (e.g. running heads called paragraph titles) now appear as ordinary labels to correct in review.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.jbig2-is-the-default-pdf-text-format-again

### Revision 1 — JBIG2 is the Freya GUI's default PDF text encoder again; truetyping is the opt-in checkbox

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.jbig2-is-the-default-pdf-text-format-again/1` · scope `path "lege-process/GUI/liminalUI/**"`, `path "lege-process/language_service/**"`

The Freya GUI's default PDF text encoder is JBIG2 symbol mode again. Truetyping stays a first-class format, keeps its name everywhere, and is offered as a checkbox (TrueTyping text) that excludes compatibility mode; clearing either checkbox returns to JBIG2. CompressionType::default() is Jbig2 and ProcessingOptions::new() starts there. The CLI is unchanged: its non-interactive default was and is ccitt4, truetyping is --truetyping or format 4.

**Context.** On the 886-page archive.org scan crusadeswholesto0000lamb_1.pdf (RGB JPEG pages), after the glyph dictionary was made parallel, the three text encoders on the same debug-fast build and machine came out at: JBIG2 33 s and 21.2 MB, CCITT4 35 s and 27.7 MB, truetyping 120 s and 45.3 MB. Truetyping is 3.6x slower and 2.1x larger than JBIG2 on a real long book, and 41 MB of its output is 22 embedded fonts: position variants, compounds and text variants use about 1000 glyph ids per page, so a 65533-id font fills every 40-odd pages and each new font re-learns the alphabet. The 20-page comparison that justified the earlier default (183 KB against 378 KB) did not see this. The user asked for the reversal on 2026-09-05 once the numbers were confirmed.

**Consequences.** Users who saved settings while truetyping was the default keep an explicit Truetyping in their saved options and stay on it until they clear the checkbox; nothing migrates them. The JBIG2 no-symbol toggle is visible again on the default path. Truetyping's remaining cost to bring down before it can be a default is glyph-id consumption per page, not matching speed.

**supersedes** `@lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-is-the-default-pdf-text-format/1`

## lege-ecosystem.decision.jbig2-symbol-substitution-is-opt-in

### Revision 1 — JBIG2 writes the bit-exact generic region unless symbol mode is asked for

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.jbig2-symbol-substitution-is-opt-in/1` · scope `path "lege-process/**"` · topic `jbig2-symbol-default`

The JBIG2 text encoder defaults to the bit-exact generic region. Symbol substitution is opt-in, and when it is asked for it is the unifying mode (Jbig2Mode::SymUnify), never the plain symbol dictionary: a plain dictionary already risks a wrong match and unification is what pays for that risk in bytes. The GUI carries a 'Symbol mode' checkbox (off by default) that sends --sym-unify; --symbol-mode and --jbig2-mode symbol still reach the middle mode from the CLI, and --no-symbol keeps working as an explicit no-op.

**Context.** Symbol substitution was the default from 2026-08-29 with --no-symbol as the opt-out. Substitution errors are silent and change words, and the user saw one in truetyping output on a bolded line ('aoil' for 'soil'). A default that can rewrite text is the wrong default for a reader-facing converter. On 41 pages of a 240-dpi book scan the generic region cost 895 KB against 878 KB for --sym-unify (1.9%), so the safe default is nearly free on noisy scans.

**Consequences.** Default JBIG2 output grows by a few percent on scans and more on clean text, where symbol matching pays best. PipelineConfig, Jbig2Settings and the interactive menu all default to Generic, so a library caller that never sets a mode now gets bit-exact output. set_jbig2_symbol_mode(true) selects SymUnify.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2-region-floor-splits-by-region-size

### Revision 1 — The verified JP2 display floor for an ordinary figure region is 65 when it covers under a quarter of the page and 70 otherwise

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2-region-floor-splits-by-region-size/1` · scope `path "lege-process/pipeline/helper_functions.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/quality_policy.rs"`

quality_policy::region_jp2_floor takes a RegionSize: an ordinary (non-HQ, non-cover) region whose pixel area is under one quarter of the output page's area gets floor 65, a larger one keeps 70; HQ (78) and cover (75) are unchanged, as are the full-page base floor (55), the grayscale region floor (65) and the legacy open-loop presets used only as fallback.

**Context.** After the jp2lam perceptual work the floor is a guaranteed display-size score rather than an open-loop preset, so the same number buys the same visible fidelity whatever the region's pixel count. The user asked on 2026-09-06 to bring the quality down a little more, about 65 for small images and 70 for big ones.

**Consequences.** Small figures cost fewer bytes; large plates and covers look as before. Size is measured on the region's placement box against the output page (RegionSize::of), threaded through region_encoding_settings and encode_region_image. Not yet measured on a corpus; the sweep in quality_policy.rs's comment covered the 70 floor only.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2lam-ssim-canonical-metric

### Revision 1 — jp2lam encode-time quality is shared JPXL SSIMULACRA2

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2lam-ssim-canonical-metric/1` · scope `path "lege-codecs/jp2lam/**"` · topic `jp2lam-ssim-controller`

jp2lam's encode-time perceptual quality target is SSIMULACRA2, using the same production implementation and metric version as JPXL (`ssimulacra2-jpxl-1` in jpegXL-rs/JPXL/crates/jpxl-perceptual). A requested score of 90.0 means the same floor in both codecs. The rust-av ssimulacra2 crate remains a test-only parity oracle. Butteraugli remains a measurement column (examples/perceptual_curve.rs and corpus screens), not the encode-time objective and not a veto. Do not introduce a second production SSIMULACRA2.

**Context.** The 2026-09-04 ssimulacrascheduler plan and the existing JPXL perceptual-quality contract. jp2lam already has perceptually weighted PCRD (local allocator) and a rust-av scoring harness. Sharing the JPXL in-tree metric is what makes a later score-matched byte comparison valid. Mixing rust-av scores with in-tree scores in one table is a known JPXL failure (jpegxl-rs.observation.pqc-pr4-rate-curve-axis-audit-2026-08-23).

**Consequences.** jp2lam depends on jpxl-perceptual (path, default-features=false). RateControl::Perceptual will take a SSIMULACRA2 score and effort, not a Butteraugli distance. Quality(u8) stays the legacy baseline until an explicit mapping session. lege-ecosystem.encode-quality.improve-photographic-rate-control's remaining 'butteraugli-anchored quality mapping' is no longer the encode-time objective.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2lam-verified-quality-scale

### Revision 1 — jp2lam quality number is the verified SSIMULACRA2 scale; legacy ladder is ApproxQuality

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2lam-verified-quality-scale/1` · scope `path "lege-codecs/jp2lam/**"` · topic `jp2lam-quality-scale`

The user-facing jp2lam quality scale is the verified SSIMULACRA2 scale: `RateControl::Quality { level, effort }` means a measured `ssimulacra2-jpxl-1` floor of `level` (0..=99, 100 = Lossless), emitting the smallest exact stream that meets it. The legacy open-loop rate ladder is preserved unchanged under `RateControl::ApproxQuality(u8)` (and the `EncodeOptions.quality` field when `rate_control` is absent) and is documented as an approximate, unmeasured preset. It is not recalibrated to the corpus bytes-per-pixel prior. `RateControl::Perceptual(PerceptualTarget)` remains the expert raw-score form. The corpus bpp-vs-score calibration is a navigation prior for the controller's first probe, never a quality definition. No legacy API compatibility is preserved (jp2lam is 0.3.x); `EncodeOptions::photo`, the photo presets and the CLI `qN` form are on the verified scale, and `--approx qN` / the auto content classifier select the legacy preset.

**Context.** User decision 2026-09-05 after the Session 8c calibration: legacy preset 80 measured SSIMULACRA2 52 at 0.8 MP, 30 at 4-6 MP and 14 at 50 MP (perceptual score 80 needs ~1.5 bpp; preset 80 spends 0.77 bpp at 0.8 MP), so an open-loop rate mapping cannot truthfully implement a unified perceptual scale and repointing it would change every consumer's sizes without the verified semantics. Supersedes the 'Quality(u8) stays the legacy baseline until an explicit mapping session' consequence of lege-ecosystem.decision.jp2lam-ssim-canonical-metric: this is that session.

**Consequences.** q80 means SSIMULACRA2 >= 80 in both JPXL and jp2lam; sizes differ by codec, meaning does not. Verified quality requires 8-bit gray/sRGB (documents, ICC and CMYK stay on ApproxQuality / explicit rate targets). The per-image feature predictor is added only if the static bpp prior cannot keep Fast in the 1-3 probe range.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.layout-model-v2-without-old-model-corrections

### Revision 1 — Lege 1.6 embeds layout model v2 and uses its boxes as they are; the old-model corrections are removed

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.layout-model-v2-without-old-model-corrections/1` · scope `path "lege-process/core/**"`, `path "lege-process/models/**"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/**"` · topic `layout-model`

Lege embeds the v2 RF-DETR-S layout model (70k hand-corrected set) in the PP-DocLayout slot and uses its detections exactly as detected. Removed: layout_correct (text boxes widened to ink and OCR lines, synthetic text and image boxes, growing image boxes to nearby ink, the inverted-page second detection pass and its LEGE_LAYOUT_IMAGE_REDETECT / LEGE_LAYOUT_OCR_DET switches), the full-page figure expansion in page_analysis with the expand_full_bleed_figure_bboxes setting, the rule that an Abandon region on a page forces JBIG2 Generic, and the line-art test (content_class) that sent image boxes judged to be drawings back to the binarized layer. An image box is a picture overlay unless it lies on substantive text. toc, reference and formula are not emitted by the model; the owner has no use for them.

**Context.** The corrections were written for PP-DocLayout-M's under-detection and for the earlier YOLO model, whose abandon class meant scan noise and whose box length was capped. Measured through Lege with v2 they lowered AP50 from 0.663 to 0.486 and swallowed 193 of 1,034 running headers and page numbers into text boxes. The line-art test decided by tone and had been tuned on grown boxes: with the model's tight boxes it binarized dark photographs into black blobs (pages 116, 136, 170 of a 200-page textbook in the first 1.6.0 tag), and repairs to it still lost light and vignetted halftones. The owner's ruling (2026-11-10): the model decides what is a picture; a line drawing kept as a picture is an accepted cost; telling figures from line art would need a model trained for it, which needs labels that do not exist. The owner also ruled out growing image boxes to the picture's edge: the tight boxes are the work the model was trained to do.

**Consequences.** Headers, footers and page numbers are Abandon (furniture) and headings are Text, so a running header the model calls a heading stays in crops and reflow: 9 of 585 on the reviewed dev pages. With the Generic rule gone, JBIG2 Symbol mode applies to ordinary book pages when the user selects it; Generic stays the default. Drawings and maps boxed as images are grayscale or colour overlays, which costs bytes: pages 1-200 of the textbook are about 13% larger than with 1.5.1, with 44 more picture overlays and none of 1.5.1's photographs lost. A box that stops a few pixels inside its picture leaves the rim to be binarized, visible as a dark edge beside the overlay. The opt-in doclayout-m feature still embeds PP-DocLayout-M, now without its corrections.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.lege-pdf-mcp-results-are-text-with-stated-coverage

### Revision 1 — lege-pdf MCP tools answer in readable text, state their coverage, and return images inline

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.lege-pdf-mcp-results-are-text-with-stated-coverage/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/agent/src/commands/mcp.rs"`, `path "lege-pdf/agent/src/commands/serve.rs"` · topic `lege-pdf-mcp-result-shape`

Every lege-pdf MCP tool returns one text block written to be read (page text under '--- page N ---' headers, one line per search match with page, box and context, tables as Markdown). response_format="json" returns compact JSON text plus structuredContent instead; text and structured content are never both sent. Each result states what it covered: pdf_text stops at max_chars (default 40000) and names the page and start_char to continue from, pdf_search stops at max_matches (default 50) and names the page to resume from, and page, byte and time limits report truncated/next_page the same way. pdf_render without an output path returns the image itself (longest edge 1568 px by default, at most 4096; PNG unless JPEG is under half its size and the PNG exceeds 300 KB; at most six pages per call; contact_sheet for more). Commands that scan and summarise (search, map, check, annotations, tables) cover every selected page unless the caller sets a page limit; the default 50-page cap applies only to commands whose output grows with every page. The Poppler-compatible front ends refuse by name any option they cannot honour rather than ignoring it.

**Context.** The first-draft server sent every result twice (JSON text mirroring structuredContent), had no budget below the 8 MiB byte cap, capped search at 50 pages while reporting it as a complete search, defaulted pdf_text to page 1, and required pdf_render to write a file the model then had to read with another tool. Measured on the 164-page T.88 spec on 2026-11-05, with response_format=json standing in for the old shape: pdf_text of pages 20-29 (31018 characters of page text) is a 31350-byte response as text and 69881 bytes as JSON plus structuredContent; page 50 alone is 1224 against 3313 bytes; pdf_search for 'Huffman' is 8089 against 29735 bytes.

**Consequences.** Clients that parsed structuredContent must pass response_format="json". The JSONL serve protocol is unchanged in being structured-only and still requires an output path for pdf_render. Text formats (the search line, the page header, the coverage warning) are now part of what agents rely on and are pinned by tests/agent_tools.rs and tests/mcp_protocol.rs.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.nup-grid-is-read-in-the-sheets-own-frame

### Revision 1 — The N-up cell grid is read in the sheet's own frame, not transposed for a landscape sheet

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.nup-grid-is-read-in-the-sheets-own-frame/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/print/src/layout.rs"`

NUp::grid() is applied to whichever way the sheet is turned, rather than being treated as portrait-relative and transposed when the sheet is landscape. A booklet is the exception: it is always two cells side by side, because the fold is always the vertical centre line.

**Context.** Transposing keeps each cell's shape fixed relative to the paper, which is the intuitive reading, but it costs paper on the two non-square grids. Measured on A4 pages onto A4 paper under FitToPage and Orientation::Auto: two-up falls from 0.707 to 0.500 and six-up from 0.354 to 0.333. The square grids -- four-, nine- and sixteen-up -- are unaffected either way.

**Consequences.** Reading the grid in the sheet's frame is also exactly the conventional CUPS arrangement: a landscape sheet with two columns for two-up, three-by-two for six-up. Orientation::Auto finds those arrangements unaided, because they score strictly better on the visible-fraction-then-coverage metric it already uses.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.pagepress-boundary-rasterizer-vs-editor

### Revision 1 — PagePress boundary: rasterizer stays in lege-process, editor suite starts in PagePress

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.pagepress-boundary-rasterizer-vs-editor/1` · scope `all`

lege-process stays the rasterizer pipeline; PagePress (sibling repo) is the start of a PDF-editor suite with its own page model, depending only on lege-pdf-write and lege-codecs via path deps.

**Context.** PagePress MVP (CLI+GUI) was built with zero references to lege-process (grep-verified). Shared ideas (margin handling, binarize, straighten) are re-implemented concepts, not copied code.

**Consequences.** Rasterizer work stays in lege-process; editor/assembly features go to PagePress. PagePress must not gain a lege-process dependency; merge stays clean.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.pipeline-memory-policy-from-external-review

### Revision 1 — Pipeline memory policy adopted from external review

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.pipeline-memory-policy-from-external-review/1` · scope `path "lege-process/core/runtime_stats.rs"`, `path "lege-process/ocr/fast.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/**"`

Adopt the review's first two changesets, adapted: (1) source-aware page admission (native dims for PDF geometry, folder headers, ZIP header sniff; post-load top-up; oversized pages admitted alone with warn-first logging, not silent clamp or error), LEGE_GPU_SESSIONS=1 honored plus a session cap at max_parallel_pages, margin pass under the same byte governor with min() concurrency and analysis-resolution PDF loads, direct InferenceHandle::detect() instead of the detached submit() wrapper, encoded-byte reservations until the writer consumes each page, and bounded blocking-drain waits on every cancel path; (2) gray-native fast OCR (no full-page RGB expansion), staged planned rendering (base, then OCR surface on demand, then one region at a time). LEGE_MEMORY_BUDGET_MB is documented as an admission setting, not an RSS promise. The runtime report (schema 2) gains GPU session count and admitted/queued MiB gauges.

**Context.** An external static review of lege-process at 883393dc (Tokio pipeline memory behavior; dagrs comparison explicitly out of scope) recommended source-aware admission, a genuine one-session GPU mode, margin/DjVu memory policy, shorter raster lifetimes, cancellation-safe reservations, and moving writer blocking work off the control thread. Verified against code at b4fb52b5: all cited behaviors were still present.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.printing-defers-prepress-to-lege-pdf-write

### Revision 1 — Office printing is built; prepress is deferred, and belongs in lege-pdf/write rather than the rasterizer

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.printing-defers-prepress-to-lege-pdf-write/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/print/**"`, `path "lege-pdf/render/**"`, `path "lege-pdf/write/**"`

lege-pdf-print implements office printing only -- paper, imposition, sheet composition, spooling -- and explicitly defers prepress: CMYK separations, an output ICC profile and rendering intent, overprint simulation, halftone screening and PDF/X conformance. When prepress is wanted, it is to be built in lege-pdf/write emitting PDF/X, not by teaching the display rasterizer to produce CMYK.

**Context.** The renderer's frozen surface contract has exactly two OutputFormat variants, Rgba8PremultipliedSrgb and Gray8; colour conversion is one-directional into sRGB by policy; and overprint is detected into a PageFeatures flag and explicitly not simulated. Every prepress want is therefore blocked on a contract-level change.

**Consequences.** A commercial printer wants a file, not a bitmap, and that file is a PDF/X -- which lege-pdf/write already has the OutputIntent and font-embedding machinery for, and which phase 0's Trim and Bleed parsing now supplies boxes to. The renderer would be involved only for on-screen soft-proofing, which is the last piece to build rather than the first.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.renderer-extracted-as-exprim

### Revision 1 — The PDF engine leaves Lege as exprim: one MIT crate in its own repository, codecs alongside

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.renderer-extracted-as-exprim/1` · scope `path "Cargo.toml"`, `path "lege-pdf/**"`, `path "lege-render-wgpu/**"`

The renderer is renamed exprim (from Latin exprimo, the owner's choice) and moved out of lege-ecosystem into the sibling repository D:/projects/exprim (Rust-projects/exprim on Linux). It publishes as ONE package, `exprim` (CRATES-IO-PLAN option A): the 21 pdf-* engine crates become modules, lege-pdf-read becomes the crate root, lege-pdf-print becomes `exprim::print` behind the `print` feature, pdf-test-support becomes `exprim::test_support` behind `test-support`. The agent CLI/MCP server becomes exprim-agent (binary `exprim`, unpublished, own workspace). jp2lam, jbig2enc-rust and djvulibrust move to exprim/codecs. The wgpu image backend and GPU postprocess executor stay in Lege as lege-render-wgpu because they need lege-gpu. Licence MIT. Lege, Liminaldoc and other siblings depend on ../exprim by path.

**Context.** Owner, 2026-11-09: 'no more lege branding for the renderer, which has taken on a life of its own'; chose one crate over an exprim-* family, chose to move it and the codecs out of lege-ecosystem, and to fold read, print and the agent in. The crates.io audit of the same day found six pdf-* names taken and path-only internal dependencies, so the graph could not publish as it stood.

**Consequences.** exprim never depends on a Lege crate (the unpublished agent's lege-ocr edge is the one exception). Lege's CI that builds against exprim needs the exprim checkout beside it. Ledger records scoped to lege-pdf/render/**, lege-pdf/read/**, lege-pdf/print/**, lege-pdf/agent/** or lege-codecs/** are history and now match no tracked path. Publication still waits on jp2lam 0.3.1 reaching crates.io.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.rfdetr-book-layout-model-replaces-doclayout-m

### Revision 1 — lege embeds the RF-DETR-S book layout model; PP-DocLayout-M is opt-in

`active` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.rfdetr-book-layout-model-replaces-doclayout-m/1` · scope `path "lege-process/Cargo.toml"`, `path "lege-process/core/lib.rs"`, `path "lege-process/models/**"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/config.rs"`

The lege executable embeds the RF-DETR-S book layout model (lege-process/models/layout-rfdetr-s.onnx,
fine-tuned on the owner's book corpus, fp16 weights, PP-DocLayout I/O contract) instead of
PP-DocLayout-M. PP-DocLayout-M is compiled in only with the opt-in `doclayout-m` feature. A
`layout.onnx` (or legacy `doclayout.onnx`) runtime asset still overrides the embedded model.
lege-document-ocr, the business-document OCR product, keeps PP-DocLayout-M: the new model was
trained only on books.

**Context.** Owner's request on 2026-11-08 ("make sure the doclayout-m is gone from compiled builds by default"), after the RF-DETR-S fine-tune beat PP-DocLayout-M on every pseudo-label metric that matters for Lege (clipping and missing text roughly halved) and lege-gpu made it fast enough (about 32 ms per page with tensor cores). The owner's gold-label review of the regression and dev sets is still pending.

**Consequences.** The lege binary grows by about 46 MB (58 MB model replacing 12 MB). Pipeline confidence threshold (0.35) and its comment were tuned for PP-DocLayout-M and may deserve retuning for RF-DETR once gold labels exist.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.sauvola-model-out-of-default-build

### Revision 1 — The Sauvola model is not embedded by default; the tileable binarizer is also the CPU fallback

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.sauvola-model-out-of-default-build/1` · scope `path "lege-process/Cargo.toml"`, `path "lege-process/color/binarization.rs"`, `path "lege-process/core/lib.rs"`

From 1.6.0 the default build embeds one heavy binarizer, the tileable one (binarizer-tilenet.onnx). It runs on the wgpu executor as before and, when the GPU is off, disabled (LEGE_HEAVY_BINARIZER=sauvolanet) or fails, on the CPU executor, padded to its stride of 8 with repeated edge pixels. sauvola.onnx is embedded only with the opt-in `sauvola-model` feature; a sauvola.prepared.onnx or sauvola.onnx runtime asset is still used as the CPU model in any build. The macOS bundle no longer ships sauvola.onnx unless SAUVOLA_ONNX is set.

**Context.** User ruling 2026-11-10: remove the Sauvola model from a default build because it is redundant with the tile binarizer. The Sauvola model was only reached as the CPU fallback of heavy binarization.

**Consequences.** Executable 0.44 MB smaller. The CPU fallback is slower: pages 20-25 of a 200-page scanned textbook with --heavy on an i7-13700H / RTX 4060 Laptop, debug-fast build: GPU tileable 3 s, CPU tileable 55 s, CPU Sauvola (sauvola-model feature) 19 s. Output size 304,606 / 304,537 / 309,216 bytes. The CPU path only runs when the GPU path is unavailable.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.sideways-pages-are-turned-upright-with-rotate

### Revision 1 — A sideways page is turned upright with /Rotate, never on its head

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.sideways-pages-are-turned-upright-with-rotate/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/write/src/artifact.rs"`, `path "lege-pdf/write/src/pages.rs"`, `path "lege-process/core/pdf_artifact.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/pdf_tokio_pipeline.rs"`

The PDF writer emits `/Rotate` on the page dictionary, and Lege sets it from the quarter turns the orientation detector already measures, so a page scanned sideways opens upright. Only the sideways turns (90 and 270) are acted on; a 180 reading is ignored. Nothing is resampled and no coordinate changes: the raster, the OCR text layer and the glyph text keep the space they were written in and turn together.

**Context.** Orientation detection has shipped since pass 6 and drives OCR (a sideways CJK scan went from 27 to about 1100 words a page), but the output was never turned: `straighten.rs` puts every glyph back where it was scanned. The user made the GUI default conditional on sideways pages being flippable in production, so the flip had to become real rather than possible. The detector calls a page sideways only when the turned page's baselines are half again as sharp as the page's own, but calls it upside down on a margin of 1.15, which is a much weaker signal.

**Consequences.** A page whose orientation nothing measured is left alone: the frame is computed for every page under truetyping, but only when OCR is on in the other text formats. `/Rotate` is written per page, never inherited from `/Pages`, so a book may mix orientations. DjVu has no equivalent attribute and would need the raster itself turned, so DjVu output is unchanged. The requested height was applied to the sideways render, so an upright page comes out taller than the device asked for.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.simple-cli-default-binarization-is-adaptive

### Revision 1 — The simple CLI mode binarizes adaptively by default, not with a fixed 180 threshold

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.simple-cli-default-binarization-is-adaptive/1` · scope `path "lege-process/core/main.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/config.rs"` · topic `cli-default-binarization`

PipelineConfig::simple_cli_defaults sets use_fixed_threshold=false so a bare `lege book.pdf` runs the Sauvola + background-normalised Otsu binarizer that the help text has always documented as the default.

**Context.** Since the initial pipeline commit the simple-mode default was a fixed threshold of 180 while --help said adaptive. Yellowed scans (crusades, globalhistory, Gernet) render their paper near gray 150, so every page came out solid black in any bilevel text format and TrueTyping saw one page-sized component and zero glyphs. The GUI, --image-debug and the music-sheet path already forced adaptive, which is why it went unnoticed. Found on 2026-09-05 while validating the review fixes.

**Consequences.** Simple-mode output on bright-paper scans changes slightly (adaptive instead of a 180 cut). --binarization threshold and --threshold still select the fixed cut explicitly. The mrc-adaptive-mask special case in main.rs that forced adaptive is now redundant but harmless.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.top-level-application-license-agpl

### Revision 2 — License the top-level Lege applications under AGPL-3.0-only

`active` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.top-level-application-license-agpl/2` · scope `path "Cargo.toml"`, `path "LICENSE"`, `path "NOTICE"`, `path "README.md"`, `path "lege-android/**"`, `path "lege-misc/docs/licenses.html"`, `path "lege-process/**"` · topic `top-level-application-license`

The Lege top-level workspace and combined application products are licensed AGPL-3.0-only, authorizing direct linking to the AGPL-3.0-only DJVULibRust crate. The root and application package metadata and included license texts must say AGPL-3.0-only. Independently usable codec and third-party subtrees retain their explicit licenses: DJVULibRust remains AGPL-3.0-only, while jbig2enc-rust and jp2lam remain MIT OR Apache-2.0.

**Context.** The user selected the plan's recommended D1 outcome: everything is AGPL again at the top level. The former MIT application declaration existed to support the now-retired arms-length subprocess boundary.

**Consequences.** Lege may restore the in-process DJVULibRust API. Application crates that directly link lege-process, including lege-android, must not continue to claim MIT. Mixed-license subtrees and third-party notices remain explicitly mapped rather than being relabeled.

**supersedes** `@lege-ecosystem.decision.top-level-application-license-agpl/1`

## lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-banks-fonts-and-respects-a-bilevel-source

### Revision 1 — A document may carry several glyph fonts, and a book already black and white is traced at its own resolution

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-banks-fonts-and-respects-a-bilevel-source/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/read/src/session.rs"`, `path "lege-pdf/write/src/**"`, `path "lege-process/encoding/glyphfont.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/config.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/pdf_tokio_pipeline.rs"`

Two changes take the ceiling off long books. A TrueType font holds 65536 glyph ids, so the session now keeps a dictionary per *bank*: a page whose components would carry the current dictionary past that limit starts the next one, every page draws from exactly one font, and the writer emits `/F2`, `/F3`, … with a reserved id per bank. And a page whose ink is already one bit — a full-page stencil, or a full-page image with a one-bit soft mask — has no more detail to give at any scale, so truetyping is rendered at that resolution rather than at its own working height. A greyscale or colour scan keeps the raised height: its soft edges resolve *better* the finer they are sampled.

**Context.** An 836-page book failed after about seven minutes with `PDF writer actor has stopped`. It was the 16-bit glyph id space: the page adapter rejects an id past 65535 and the writer actor died on it, while the real message was lost because the sender only sees a closed channel. The same run was slow for a second reason — the book was itself a Lege output, a greyscale JP2 under a JBIG2 stencil at 1200 px, and rendering it at 2400 invented interpolated edges that no two impressions of a letter shared: 120 pages made 24 381 glyphs in 3 minutes at 2400 px and 9 363 in 18 seconds at 1400.

**Consequences.** The book now finishes in 3 minutes with two fonts. The writer actor records what it died of before dropping its receiver, so a page worker reports the cause rather than the symptom. Bank assignment is decided before a page is analysed, from the component count plus headroom, so a page never straddles two fonts and no composite ever crosses one. `GlyphFontSession::with_prototype_cap` exists so the split can be tested without 65 000 shapes.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-is-the-default-pdf-text-format

### Revision 2 — Truetyping is the name and the default for PDF text output

`superseded` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-is-the-default-pdf-text-format/2` · scope `path "lege-process/GUI/Freya/**"`, `path "lege-process/color/color_processing.rs"`, `path "lege-process/core/main.rs"`, `path "lege-process/language_service/**"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/config.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/pdf_tokio_pipeline.rs"`

The glyph-font text format is called `truetyping` in every user-facing surface and is the default PDF text encoder in the Freya GUI. `glyphfont` stays an accepted spelling of the CLI and config value forever, normalized at parse time, so scripted runs and saved settings keep working; the Rust module, the log prefixes and the AKR history keep the name they were built under, because they name the mechanism rather than the product. In the GUI the two text-encoder opt-outs are checkboxes that exclude each other by construction: `CompressionType` gained a `Truetyping` variant and is now the single field the text encoder is read from, so JBIG2 and compatibility mode (CCITT4 + baseline JPEG) cannot both be on, and clearing either returns to truetyping. Detected image regions are a separate three-way choice: Original, Dithered, or JBIG2 halftone. Halftone remains available with either truetyping or JBIG2 text and is embedded as its own JBIG2 overlay; compatibility mode and DjVu do not offer it.

**Context.** Seven passes brought the format to parity: on a 20-page scan it is 183 KB against JBIG2 symbol mode's 378 KB at equal or better legibility, and the user signed off on the rendered outputs. The old `effective_text_format` derived the encoder from `image_processing_type` whenever layout analysis was on, so the GUI's real default was CCITT4 and the compatibility checkbox's `compression_type` flip was a no-op on the default path. Making the text encoder an explicit field removes that coupling: how image regions are treated no longer decides how text is written.

**Consequences.** Text encoding and detected-image encoding remain orthogonal. Choosing Dithered or JBIG2 halftone does not switch the text encoder; the halftone choice stays visible with truetyping and JBIG2 text, while compatibility mode keeps its CCITT4 + baseline-JPEG promise and DjVu keeps its native image path. Raster reflow re-renders every page as an image and has no text encoder, so it refuses truetyping on the CLI and is not offered it in the GUI. The Freya GUI is the only frontend changed: the sheet-music GUI and lege-viewer carry their own copies of the option model and keep the old default.

**supersedes** `@lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-is-the-default-pdf-text-format/1`

## lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-leaves-bilevel-sources-alone

### Revision 1 — Truetyping is skipped when the source's ink is already one bit; source masks pass through

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-leaves-bilevel-sources-alone/1` · scope `path "lege-process/encoding/glyphfont.rs"`, `path "lege-process/pipeline/**"`

A source page whose ink already comes from a one-bit image or a one-bit soft mask (a JBIG2 or CCITT text layer, an MRC mask) is original text: truetyping does not trace it. If the sampled pages of a document are mostly bilevel (bilevel_source_height), the run switches its text format to jbig2 before any page is processed and gives back the height the caller asked for; a single bilevel page in a scanned book drops its glyph session and is encoded as the jbig2 format would (page_ink_is_bilevel); and a preserved JBIG2 SMask passes through untouched under truetyping exactly as it does under jbig2 and ccitt4.

**Context.** The preserved-mask path already passed the source mask through for jbig2 and ccitt4, but truetyping replaced it with glyph text traced from the decoded mask, and a plain bilevel book was traced at its own resolution. Tracing one-bit ink can only move its edges, and the font it makes is a lossy copy of something the input already held losslessly.

**Consequences.** Truetyping on a lege JBIG2 output is a JBIG2 re-encode at the requested height (20 pages: 0.56 MB in 8 s). clamp_truetyping_render_height is gone; set_text_format restores the requested height when leaving truetyping. Implemented 2026-09-06 in lege-process/pipeline/pdf_tokio_pipeline.rs and config.rs.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-renders-in-grayscale-by-default

### Revision 1 — Truetyping renders its ink mask through the MRC clean path

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.truetyping-renders-in-grayscale-by-default/1` · scope `path "lege-process/**"` · topic `truetyping-render-mode`

Choosing truetyping selects grayscale/MRC rendering. In the CLI, --text-format truetyping implies --grayscale unless a bilevel mode is named (--binarization, --threshold, --sauvola-k); in the GUI, ticking TrueTyping flips the Binarized/Grayscale pair to Grayscale, which the user can flip back.

**Context.** Truetyping draws the text as outlines over a background, so the ink mask only decides where the outlines go. Sauvola on a raw scan keeps the paper grain and every speck becomes a glyph; the MRC clean path despeckles it. On 41 pages of the crusades scan: 0.77 MB and 1347 shapes grayscale against 2.56 MB and 13087 bilevel, and the grayscale run was faster. Tested on a Kobo Clara BW: both load and page-turn acceptably, grayscale is considerably smaller.

**Consequences.** Bilevel truetyping stays reachable by naming a binarization mode or unticking Grayscale. Truetyping remains opt-in overall (see @lege-ecosystem.decision.jbig2-is-the-default-pdf-text-format-again): dictionary matching still makes occasional substitution errors on bold text.

## lege-ecosystem.decision.vulkan-replaces-dx12

### Revision 1 — Lege runs on Vulkan (Metal on macOS); Direct3D 12 is removed

`active` · `@lege-ecosystem.decision.vulkan-replaces-dx12/1` · scope `path "lege-gpu/Cargo.toml"`, `path "lege-gpu/src/vision/runtime/device.rs"`, `path "lege-gpu/src/wgpu_setup.rs"`

Lege's GPU work runs on Vulkan on Windows, Linux and Android, and on Metal on macOS. The Direct3D 12
backend is removed from every build (lege-gpu no longer enables wgpu's dx12 or static-dxc features);
WGPU_BACKEND accepts only vulkan, metal or all, and ignores anything else with a warning. On Vulkan
adapters that report 16x16x16 f16->f32 cooperative matrices, GEMMs run on tensor cores.

**Context.** Owner's decision on 2026-11-08 after the tensor-core work: DX12 had been the Windows default on the belief that it was faster. Measured on the owner's RTX 4060 Laptop, Vulkan matched or beat it on every Lege workload (RF-DETR-S layout 42 vs 48 ms per page on f32 kernels, 32 ms with tensor cores; a 200-page Structures job 42 vs 48-54 s; a 200-page heavy-binarization scan job equal), outputs agreed (Structures 200/200 pages pixel-identical at 100 dpi, sahib 194/200 with the worst page 0.12% of pixels at the binarizer threshold), and wgpu reaches tensor cores only through Vulkan.

**Consequences.** Windows builds no longer need Microsoft's DXC compiler or the Visual Studio ATL component. A machine whose driver has no Vulkan support loses GPU processing (layout detection is disabled and the CPU paths run); the old GL fallback was never compiled in, so pre-Vulkan Intel iGPUs had no GPU path before either. Speed evidence is from one NVIDIA laptop; AMD and Intel Vulkan drivers on Windows are unmeasured. On macOS the choice between wgpu's Metal backend and CoreML is open.

## lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.final-buffer-ownership

### Revision 1 — Allocate renderer and JPEG final buffers in their shared Arc layout

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.final-buffer-ownership/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/render/crates/pdf-image/src/jpeg/**"`, `path "lege-pdf/render/crates/pdf-render-cpu/**"` · topic `final-buffer-ownership`

Allocate CPU page surfaces and JPEG decoded output directly as uniquely-owned Arc slices, mutate them only while unique, and hand the Arc to HostPage or DecodedImage without a whole-buffer Vec-to-Arc conversion. Preserve Surface clone value semantics by deep-copying knockout-group snapshots.

## lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.gray8-draws-take-the-rgb8-fast-paths

### Revision 1 — Gray8 image draws take the axis-aligned RGB8 fast paths through a one-time promotion; reduced-resolution decodes are cached by their decode level

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.gray8-draws-take-the-rgb8-fast-paths/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/read/src/session.rs"`, `path "lege-pdf/render/crates/pdf-render-cpu/**"`

In `paint_image`, an opaque, normal-blend, unclipped, axis-aligned 8-bit gray image with no `/Decode` and no colour-key mask is re-expressed once as RGB8 (`PreparedImage::gray8_promoted_to_rgb8`: each byte tripled straight into the shared allocation, colour space marked RGB, everything else cloned) before the fast-path eligibility tests, so the nearest, bilinear, area-minified and masked area-minified RGB8 painters apply to it. `pixel()` answers `[g, g, g, 255]` for such a gray texel and `[r, g, b, 255]` for RGB8, so the promoted draw is byte-identical to the RGB8 twin by construction (test `gray8_draws_match_their_rgb8_twins`). Colour-keyed gray images are not promoted (B5, 2026-11-08: the one-pair key was rejected after promotion). A magnified draw under a mask has no fast path either way and is not expanded. Separately, `ImageCacheKey` keys DCT and JPX entries by the codec's reported decode level and by the declared colour space (B1, 2026-11-08, branch jolly-ride); JBIG2 and CCITT payloads are the same whatever the draw size and are keyed without a level, so a page rendered at two sizes decodes them once.

**Context.** The existing fast paths (@lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.mrc-masked-draw-fast-path) accepted only RGB8 and CMYK sources. Scanned books and Lege's own MRC output are 8-bit DeviceGray almost without exception, so every page draw of Lege's main workload was taking the generic per-pixel sampler at roughly 250 ns per destination pixel: 1.0 s for a 1697x2400 page, 0.4 s at 1200 px, and the analysis render on top. Lege renders each page twice (bounded analysis render, then the output render), and the JBIG2 mask was decoded for both because the cache key carried the target size. The 2026-11-08 scoping review then found that DCT also decodes at a reduced scale chosen from the target, so a key without the level served a quarter-area decode to the base render (B1).

**Consequences.** Gobineau (MRC source: gray JPX foreground and background, JBIG2 SMask), 20 pages, per-stage CPU: output render 22.7 s -> 3.0 s at 2400 px and 8.1 s -> 1.7 s at 1200 px; analysis render 6.2 s -> 2.3 s; the shared image cache went from 0 hits to one hit per page. The promotion costs one 3x copy of the source per draw (a 6 Mpx page: about 5 ms and 18 MiB transient, halved by writing into the final Arc on 2026-11-08), capped at 64 Mpx like the CMYK conversion. The ring caveat below was confirmed and left as the PDFium-matching behaviour on 2026-11-08 (dev-notes/lege-pdf/render-refinement/scoping-20261108/measurements/image-edge-ring-pdfium-probe-20261108.md).

**Retired claims** — `#promotion-is-exact`, `#target-only-for-jpx`, dropped at this revision.

## lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.mrc-masked-draw-fast-path

### Revision 1 — MRC pages are shading-bound, not decode-bound: masked area-min fast path in pdf-render-cpu

`proposed` · `@lege-ecosystem-perf.renderer.mrc-masked-draw-fast-path/1` · scope `path "lege-pdf/render/crates/pdf-render-cpu/**"`

Add `paint_axis_aligned_rgb8_area_min_masked` to `pdf-render-cpu/src/exec.rs`: an axis-aligned area-minification fast path for RGB8 image draws carrying a bilevel cut-out, covering both MRC mask encodings (1-bit `/SMask` coverage layer, and hard `/Mask` over an `/ImageMask` stencil). Per-column and per-row preparation of the inverse map, the base box-filter taps, and the mask's per-axis lookup replaces per-pixel recomputation. Byte-identical to the generic path, edge anti-aliasing included. Measured 2026-08-08; full record in lege-pdf/render/docs/refinement/performance-history/optimization-mrc-mask-20260808.md
